findings.where: Article page specimen, the three-item list under 'So, what are the key chapter topics?' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The list loses the article's line spacing. The paragraphs above it have generous leading (about 19/30), but the list items have almost none. Each wrapped line touches the next, and at phone width items like 'a chapter on Institutional / Coordination and Responsibilities; / and' run together into one grey block. You can only tell where one item ends and the next begins by the bullets.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Angélique: the brief asks for type on a rhythm that holds when she adds a list, and the specimen shows it breaking on its first list. Mark's readers at the development banks would also find the list harder to read than the prose around it.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the subhead 'So, what are the key chapter topics?' against the article title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' (worst on phone)
findings.fault: The subhead is set as large and as heavy as the article title, and at phone width it is visibly larger than the title. Nothing in size or weight marks it as a section inside the article. It reads as a second article starting.
findings.who_objects: A reader skimming the article, who uses the title and subheads to see its structure. Angélique, who needs a subhead style that clearly ranks below the title when she adds more of them.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the photo caption 'A television studio interview. Placeholder…' and the subhead below it (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The subhead sits right under the caption with almost no space, while the space below the subhead is wider. So the subhead groups with the caption above it, not with the section it introduces, and the caption reads like a line of the heading.
findings.who_objects: Readers, who would read the caption and subhead as one unit. The founder, because the brief's test is that spacing holds when an image, caption and subhead are added, and here it is out of rhythm at exactly that join.

findings.where: First screen, the large ghost 'PPP' letters behind Mark's heading (desktop), and the cropped 'PP' behind the heading at phone width
findings.fault: Giant pale serif letters sit right behind the first two lines of the heading. Their strokes cross 'In my view, we are at' and 'a turning point', which muddies the one line meant to be read first. On the phone they are cropped into an unreadable blur behind the heading.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges the first screen first and asked for one very large serif line with scale contrast, not more elements. A visitor, who sees a smudge behind Mark's words rather than a clean line.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the PDF link 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' and the list bullets
findings.fault: The link and the bullets are set in an orange-red. That colour is in neither the palette nor the text-pair table, which say 'four colours and no accent' and give links as house blue, as 'Play again' is. Like links are not set alike, and a colour that marks a link also colours the bullets, which are not links.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for blue and grey as the only ink. Readers, who learn on this page that blue means a link and then meet a red one.

findings.where: Motion sketch specimen, the heading 'placed, calm, exact'
findings.fault: It is set as a large light Source Sans display line. The type-pair specimen gives the sans only to the nav, the action, captions, dates and labels, and gives display lines to Gelasio. The tile adds a third heading style that its own type rules do not include.
findings.who_objects: The founder, comparing the type pair's stated roles with the page and finding a display sans that reads closer to the 'techy' look the brief rules out.

findings.where: Article page specimen, the apostrophe in the title 'The World's Best'
findings.fault: The title uses a straight typewriter apostrophe, while the subhead and the body use curly quotation marks (‘chapter topics’, “What is…”). Like marks are not set alike, and the straight one stands out at display size.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, such as a lawyer or a development-bank editor, for whom a straight quote in a display title looks unedited.
